This is accomplished by achieving temperatures >1000 ◦ C and pressures ~1000 atm around the bubble, cre- ating a powerful destructive force (Awoyemi et  al. 2024). High- frequency ultrasound has been demonstrated in previ- ous studies to mineralize PFAS in laboratory- scale reactors, creating fluoride and carbon dioxide without producing problematic by- products (Kewalramani et  al. 2022). Fol- lowing the success of these bench level demonstrations of PFAS destruction in solid–liquid slurries, high- frequency ultrasound technology can be evaluated as an energetically efficient treatment option for larger scale treatment, such as the on- site treatment of groundwater from contaminated sites. Calculation of PFAS Degradation Efficiency Degradation efficiency serves as the primary metric to evaluate the effectiveness of PFAS destruction by ultrasound treatment. The degradation efficiency denotes the degree to which the PFAS were destroyed during the ultrasound treatment. A high degradation efficiency indicates a high destruction level of PFAS and thus an effective treatment process. The small volume capacity of the system (100 L) remains a limitation, and so a larger scale study is recommended next following the successful demonstration presented in this study. It will be important to demonstrate that both efficiency and destructive performance can be main- tained as treatment volume increases to give this technology the best chance to effectively serve end users. Lastly, future research should consider evaluating gas- phase intermediate compounds that may be formed during ultrasonic treatment to fully evaluate the fluorine mass balance. Overall, this ultrasound technology was proven to be an effective treatment for the destruction of PFAS in highly contaminated groundwater within a source zone with little evidence of the formation of problematic by- products while achieving an order of magnitude decrease in concentration. We recommend additional experimentation to evaluate this technology to destroy pure AFFF or media contaminated with novel and/or replacement PFAS not evaluated in this study (Yan et al. 2015; McCord et al. 2020; Tenorio et  al. 2020). The objectives of this study are to (i) implement an inno- vative ultrasound technology to treat PFAS- laden ground- water within source zones at impacted sites; (ii) evaluate and optimize critical parameters such as power density and residence time to achieve maximum degradation efficiency of PFAS; (iii) characterize the PFAS groundwater influent for PFAS, organics, and inorganics and assess whether the parameters may impact treatment efficiency; (iv) quantify the degradation efficiency for precursors, long- chain, and short- chain PFAS; and (v) monitor the mass balance of fluo- rine to determine if PFAS have been mineralized completely without creating PFAS as byproducts. The innovation in this application includes the use of high- frequency ultrasound combined with the number and orientation of the transduc- ers. The described new radial plasma discharge reactor (RAP) performed remarkably well in treating water contaminated by common PFAS surfactants perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) and perfluorooctyl sulfonate (PFOS) with respect to most significant process indicators: degradation kinetics, conversion extent, amount of byproducts and energy consumption. KEYWORDS: foam fractionation, electrochemical oxidation, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, landfill leachate, groundwater, numerical modeling ■ INTRODUCTION The widespread presence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), particularly in the aquatic environment, has become a global cause for concern. 1−4 PFAS originate from various sources like the use of aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF), industrial releases, landfilling of PFAS-containing waste, and atmospheric deposition. 5−7 Additionally, the breakdown of less mobile perfluoroalkyl acid (PFAA) precursor compounds leads to increasing levels of mobile short-chain PFAS. 8 Commonly, perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA, C n F 2n+1 COOH) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA, C n F 2n+1 SO 3 H) are considered short-chained for carbon chain lengths (n) below seven and six, respectively. 9 For the two most well-known PFAS, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS), adverse health effects have been described extensively.

However, the previous use of PFAS-formulated AFFF has led to sig - nificant environmental contamination, as PFAS from these foams can leach into groundwater, surface water, and soil [ 7 ]. Various re - mediations are being developed and employed. For example, foam fractionation, a separation process happening at the gas-liquid interface, has been explored as a remediation technique for concentrating and removing PFAS from aqueous solutions, including groundwater, landfill leachate and AFFF [ 8 , 9 ]. This process generates foam fractionate (FF), a concentrated phase of PFAS that can be further treated [ 10 ], such as via PFAS degradation to mitigate their environmental impact eventually [ 9 ]. However, the persistent nature of PFAS and their widespread dis - tribution necessitate effective degradation strategies, including elec - trochemistry [ 11 ], plasma [ 12 ], ball milling [ 13 ] and thermal destruction [ 14 ]. Ultrasonication has emerged as a promising PFAS degradation technique. It utilises high-frequency sound waves to create acoustic cavitation, which involves the intense formation and collapse of bubbles that generate the localised hot spots with temperatures near 5000 K and

cavitation, which involves the intense formation and collapse of bubbles that generate the localised hot spots with temperatures near 5000 K and pressures over 1000 atm [ 15 , 16 ]. These extreme conditions lead to two primary degradation pathways: (i) indirect degradation by reactive radicals, such as hydroxyl radical (OH • ) and hydrogen radical (H • ) generated from water vapour and (ii) direct pyrolysis through thermal decomposition, as detailed in our prior work [ 10 ]. However, dissolved ions present in the water and at the interface can affect radical gener - ation [ 18 ], possibly suppressing cavitation, scavenging reactive species, and altering bubble dynamics, ultimately reducing degradation effi - ciency. The specific effects of these interactions remain unclear and require further investigation, as examined in this study. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) have previously been formulated as integral components in many industrial and consumer products due to their remarkable properties, including water and oil resistance, as well as exceptional thermal and chemical stability [ 1 ]. These attributes make PFAS invaluable in applications ranging from firefighting foams to non-stick coatings, contributing significantly to technological advancements. Various PFAS compounds have been detected in numerous environmental matrices [ 2 ], raising significant concerns due to their persistence, bioaccumulation, and potential adverse health effects such as cancer development and thyroid hormone destruction [ 3 ]. PFAS contamination in environmental water bodies is particularly alarming as it poses risks to both the ecosystem and human health [ 4 ]. A recent study found PFAS, including PFOA (mean range 2.8 – 17.7 ppt) and PFOS (mean range 5.8 – 19.7 ppt), in Australian es - tuaries, with higher concentrations in creek water (CW) than in river water [ 5 ], highlighting their widespread presence in aquatic environ - ments. Among the various sources of PFAS, aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) is notable, particularly when considering that PFAS have been formulated as the key ingredients before. AFFF has been extensively used for firefighting in situations involving flammable liquid fires, due

and reduces environmental impact [ 15 , 19 ]. Compared to other tech - nologies such as electrochemical oxidation, photochemical degradation, plasma treatment, and microwave-based processes, ultrasonication may also yield fewer ultrashort-chain by-products. Nonetheless, challenges remain around operational parameters, energy input and scalability, as discussed in earlier work [ 17 ], beyond the ionic background. In addition to these controllable factors, water matrix properties such as ionic composition, conductivity, and total organic carbon (TOC) can also play a critical role in determining degradation outcomes. Given that seawater (SW), freshwater (e.g., CW), and groundwater (GW) exhibit distinct ionic profiles [ 20 ], understanding how these matrices affect PFAS degradation is crucial for optimising treatment methods across diverse water types and advancing their scale-up for real-world applications. Building on our previous work on ultrasonication of PFAS, AFFF, and FF [ 10 ], this study investigates the impact of ionic composition and water chemistry on the ultrasonication degradation of PFAS by spiking perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), 6:2 fluorotelomer sulfonate (6:2 FTS), AFFF, and FF in SW and CW. Outside of the United States, only limited evaluations of removal‐based methods exist, such as flocculation/precipitation methods studied in Germany (Maga et al. 2021 ) and membrane bioreactor treatment of landfill leachate in China (Feng et al. 2021 ). The scope of the applied sustainability dimensions varied across these studies. Environmental life cycle assessment (LCA) has been the dominant sustainability dimension, focusing largely on energy intensity, carbon footprints, and toxic emissions. A handful of works integrated economic aspects, mainly in the form of cost analyses for adsorbent regeneration, energy con - sumption, or system operation (Moeini et al. 2022 ; Ellis et al. 2023 ). Meanwhile, social dimensions remain the least investigated, incorporating structured tools such as the Social Sustainability Evaluation Matrix (SSEM) (Reddy et al. 2014 ). Moreover, the reported case studies applied a comprehensive sustainability assessment only to the removal phase, with limited consideration of downstream destruction methods. Although various technologies have been investigated for PFAS degradation (Kewalramani et al. 2022 ; Ross et al. 2018 ), only incineration/thermal degradation has already been deployed in the industry (Meegoda et al. 2022 ). Nonetheless, there is a lack of studies comparing the performance of various destruction methods in terms of sustainability metrics to shed light on the most promising methods for future scalability. A comprehen - sive sustainability assessment, based on the triple bottom line framework, can evaluate outcomes of these methods across environmental, social, and economic criteria. In UVAOP treatment, water passes through a reactor vessel equipped with lamps that emit UV light (USEPA 2016 ). In photolysis, the contaminants are degraded by the photons emitted by the UV lamps. Alternatively, advanced oxidation involves the addition of chemicals such as hydrogen peroxide, sodium persulfate, or chlorine. These chemicals react with UV light to generate radicals, such as hydroxyl and persulfate, which in turn oxidize contaminants, including PFAS. Although background datasets (e.g., energy production and materials manufacturing) include inherent uncertainty, these values were applied consistently across all three PFAS destruction methods. Additionally, the relative differences between technologies are driven by large variations in energy demand and reagent use. Thus, the comparative conclusions are expected to remain qualitatively valid despite unquantified uncertainty. While this study focused on conventional incineration pro - cesses, recent studies have developed alternative thermal PFAS destruction technologies, such as joule heating (Scotland et al. 2025 ) and induction heating (Xiao et al. 2023 ). These approaches achieve complete PFAS mineralization through rapid, localized heating, resulting in lower energy consumption and improved cost efficiency compared to conventional incin - eration. Thus, future studies may investigate the sustainability of these advanced thermal degradation in PFAS applications. In the case of EO for PFAS destruction, the choice of electrode material and its selectivity play a critical role in determining the overall performance, energy consumption, and environmental footprint. Not all the electrical current supplied to an EO reactor goes toward target contaminant degradation. Due to their distinct structure, PFAS are regarded as chemically and thermally stable, meaning that higher temperatures and extended residence times are required to achieve an adequate level of destruction. Inciner - ation is recognized as a thermal oxidation treatment method and takes place in an oxygen‐abundant environment at elevated tem - peratures. The majority of hazardous waste incinerators function within a temperature range of 980°C–1200°C. As the thermal breakdown of most organic materials happens within the range of 590°C–650°C, it is anticipated that almost complete elimination of the organic substances in the waste will be achieved, which includes PFAS (> 99.9%) (Meegoda et al. 2022 ). 2.2 | Electrochemical Oxidation The electrochemical destruction technique applies an electrical current to oxidize or reduce organic contaminants by passing it through a conductive solution established between an anode and a cathode. The contaminants are either absorbed and broken down at the electrode or in the surrounding liquid medium (Leung et al. 2022 ). The EO method has been demonstrated to transform PFAS compounds into environmentally harmless by‐ products through direct and indirect reactions. economic, and social aspects of the destruction methods. Environmental consequences are evaluated through a life cycle assessment (LCA) implemented in SimaPro. Economic sustainability is assessed by analyzing direct and indirect costs. Social implications are evaluated using the Social Sustainability Evaluation Matrix (SSEM). Furthermore, the Integrated Value Model for Sustainability Assessment (MIVES) is used to integrate the results of environmental, economic, and social sustainability assessments. Prior studies have demonstrated that PFASs can be defluorinated and mineralized by high frequency ultrasound [25,31 – 34] .
